analysis.one_liner: Raises the estate tax on the largest inheritances and closes trust loopholes used to avoid it.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee in June 2015 and never received a hearing, markup, or floor vote before the 114th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would restore a stricter estate tax: it would lower the untaxed estate threshold back to $3.5 million per person, raise rates to 55% on estates above $50 million, and add a 10% surtax on estates above $500 million [S2]. It would also close several techniques wealthy families use to avoid the tax, including certain short-term trusts, long-lived 'dynasty' trusts, and valuation discounts that shrink the reported value of family businesses [S2][S3]. It pairs those increases with larger protections for family farmland and for conservation easement donors [S2][S3].
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary taxpayers benefit indirectly, because a broader estate tax raises federal revenue that can fund services or reduce borrowing. Directly, the bill helps two narrower groups: families inheriting working farmland, whose taxable valuation would get a much larger discount that grows with inflation, and landowners who donate conservation easements, whose exclusion would rise to $2 million [S2][S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Taxpayers overall, plus farm families and land donors

how_it_helps.text: Restores the estate tax exemption to $3.5 million per person and raises the top rate to 55% on estates over $50 million, with a 10% surtax on estates over $500 million, increasing federal revenue from the largest inheritances [S2][S3].

Raises the special valuation reduction for qualifying family farmland from $750,000 to $3 million and indexes it for inflation, making it easier for heirs to keep working farms rather than sell land to pay the tax [S2][S3].
Increases the estate tax exclusion for donated conservation easements to $2 million and to 60% of the land's value, encouraging land preservation [S2][S3].

Requires heirs to report inherited property values consistently with the estate tax return and closes avoidance tools including short-term GRAT trusts, grantor trusts, minority-interest valuation discounts, and indefinite 'dynasty' trusts, limiting tax avoidance by the wealthiest families [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Families with estates above $3.5 million would pay higher taxes, with the steepest rates on estates over $10 million, $50 million, and $500 million. Wealth management, trust, and estate-planning professionals would lose business as several avoidance structures stop working [S2][S3].
analysis.who_pays_short: Very large estates and estate planners

drawbacks.text: The bill taxes estates starting at $3.5 million, which captures some family-owned businesses and farms; the farm and easement provisions soften but do not eliminate the risk that heirs must sell assets to pay the tax [S2][S3].

The new basis-reporting and valuation rules add compliance paperwork for executors, gift donors, and small business owners transferring interests, an administrative cost honest supporters would acknowledge [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The cost falls almost entirely on the largest estates — the top rate changes apply above $10 million and the surtax above $500 million — while the farm and easement provisions specifically protect heirs of working land [S2][S3]. The main honest objection is complexity and the risk to heirs of illiquid family businesses, which the bill partially addresses but does not fully solve.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the House Ways and Means Committee on June 25, 2015, and the committee took no further action on it for the rest of the 114th Congress, so it died without a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote [S5].

narrative.text: Rep. Janice Schakowsky (D-IL) introduced the bill on June 25, 2015, joined by Rep. Keith Ellison (D-MN) [S1][S5].
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means, which holds jurisdiction over estate tax legislation [S5].
One cosponsor, Rep. Ellison, is listed for the bill [S4].
The action history shows no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor action after the referral through the end of the Congress on January 3, 2017 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Families with the largest estates, who would have paid the higher tax, and the trust and estate-planning industry, whose avoidance structures would have been closed, were spared because the bill never advanced. Advocates of a stronger estate tax gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Very large estates and estate planners

for.name: Rep. Janice Schakowsky
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill in the House on June 25, 2015.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, estate tax jurisdiction
against.what_they_did: Never held a hearing or markup on the bill after the June 2015 referral, leaving it to die without action.

against.name: Paul Ryan
against.role: Chair, House Ways and Means (until October 2015), then Speaker
against.what_they_did: His committee took up no estate tax increase legislation in the 114th Congress; he moved from the chairmanship to the Speakership during the bill's window and the Republican majority did not schedule estate tax increases for a vote.

sides.party_line_note: The only two sponsors were Democrats, and the Republican-controlled Ways and Means Committee took no action; no roll-call vote was ever recorded [S3][S4][S5].

industries.industry: Very wealthy families with estates over $3.5 million
industries.note: The bill would restore the $3.5 million exemption, raise rates to 55% above $50 million, and add a 10% surtax above $500 million, directly increasing taxes on the largest inheritances [S2][S3].

industries.industry: Trust and estate planning, wealth management, and appraisal services
industries.note: The bill would shut down or restrict several fee-generating avoidance structures: short-term GRATs, grantor trusts, minority-interest valuation discounts, indefinite dynasty trusts, and aggressive gift exclusions for illiquid interests [S2][S3].
The special farmland valuation reduction would quadruple to $3 million and be indexed for inflation, easing the estate tax burden on heirs of working farms [S2][S3].

industries.industry: Land trusts and conservation easement donors
industries.note: The estate tax exclusion for donated conservation easements would rise to $2 million and 60% of land value, making land preservation more attractive [S2][S3].
